meta.title: The accountability ledger
meta.note: Persons and companies named in the record, with what a court, a government or a shareholder has actually done about them. Statements are joined from the statements file, the sections are found in the report itself, and the sanctions are the measures on the world-positions file. Nothing on this page is asserted that is not already somewhere else on this site.
meta.source: report-final.md; data/statements.json; data/world-positions.json; Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, Articles 86, 89(1) and 127(1)

classes.label: Israeli government
classes.note: Ministers, the President and members of the Knesset — the level at which the specific intent for genocide has to be proved, and the level at which it was spoken aloud.

classes.label: Israeli military command
classes.note: Officers who commanded, spoke for or administered the campaign. Command responsibility under Article 28 of the Rome Statute attaches to what a commander knew and failed to prevent, not only to what he ordered.

classes.label: Allied governments
classes.note: Officials of the states that supply the weapons, the money and the diplomatic cover, whose own words are part of the record.

classes.label: Corporate actors
classes.note: Executives of the companies whose products, platforms and finance the documented conduct runs on, quoted where they have spoken about that use themselves.

classes.label: The accountability machinery
classes.note: Judges, prosecutors and mandate holders who pursued the case — and who were sanctioned by a permanent member of the Security Council for doing so.

classes.label: Palestinian armed groups
classes.note: Those against whom the same court sought warrants for the crimes of 7 October, held to the same standard and listed in the same place.

classes.label: Israeli and Jewish dissent
classes.note: Former prime ministers, former security chiefs, historians and writers who put the finding on the record from inside the community it is said to injure.

classes.label: The founding record
classes.note: Figures of the movement and of the state before 2023, quoted because the pattern they describe is the one the report documents continuing.

companies.supplies: Signed a strategic partnership with the Israeli Ministry of Defence in January 2024 to supply data-analytics software for what the company described as war-related missions.
companies.note: The chief executive, Alex Karp, has said publicly that the product is used, on occasion, to kill people, and told a protester at the Hill & Valley Forum in May 2025 that those killed were "mostly terrorists, that's true". Palantir disputed Amnesty's characterisation. The same company holds at least 34 UK government contracts worth at least £670 million since 2020, including the £330 million NHS Federated Data Platform and a £240.6 million uncompeted Ministry of Defence contract; on 3 June 2026 the Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee recommended that the government exercise the February 2027 break clause and replace it.

companies.name: SpaceX (Starlink)
companies.supplies: The satellite network that was the only alternative to Gaza's repeatedly severed terrestrial communications.
companies.note: On 27 November 2023 Elon Musk agreed with Israel's Communications Minister Shlomo Karhi that Starlink would operate in Gaza only with the approval of the Israeli Ministry of Communications. By February 2024 the single authorised deployment was a terminal serving the Emirati field hospital in Rafah.

companies.name: Google
companies.supplies: Co-holder, with Amazon, of the $1.2 billion Project Nimbus cloud contract with the Israeli government, under terms that forbid restricting military use even where it breaches the company's own terms of service.
companies.note: An internal Google risk assessment, reported by The Intercept on 12 May 2025, found the company knew before signing that it could not control military use of the technology; its own consultant recommended withholding machine-learning and AI tools from the Israeli military. Google supplied the full suite regardless and said "nothing has changed."

positions.name: Hungary
positions.detail: Hosted Netanyahu in April 2025 in breach of its obligation to cooperate, a non-compliance finding referred to the Assembly of States Parties, then reversed course: the National Assembly voted 133–37 on 27 May 2026 to repeal the exit law, and Prime Minister Péter Magyar committed to arresting Netanyahu if he visits.

positions.detail: Netanyahu skipped Davos in 2026 rather than enter a state party.

positions.name: South Korea
positions.detail: President Lee Jae Myung called Netanyahu a war criminal in May 2026 and ordered the government to assess issuing an arrest warrant in line with the ICC's.

positions.name: France
positions.detail: Barred Ben-Gvir from entry in May 2026.

positions.name: Poland
positions.detail: Passed a government resolution guaranteeing Netanyahu safe entry for the Auschwitz commemoration — itself a breach of the Rome Statute.

positions.name: United States
positions.detail: Not a party to the Rome Statute. The American Service-Members' Protection Act of 2002 bars federal and state cooperation with the Court, and President Trump stated on 20 July 2026 that Netanyahu "will not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form" in the United States.

positions.name: Türkiye
positions.detail: Not a party, but submitted a request to Interpol on 21 August 2026 for a Red Notice against Netanyahu. Interpol's constitution bars acting on requests of a predominantly political character, and no notice had issued.

icc.note: All 125 states parties are bound by Article 86 to cooperate fully with the Court and by Article 89(1) to comply with a request for arrest and surrender. A withdrawal notified under Article 127(1) takes effect one year later, so each of the five states that has given notice remains bound throughout that year.
